title: Enhance EV station charge and discharge based on deep learning forecasting method incorporating renewable energy sources and multi-objective optimization algorithm
journal: International Journal of Renewable Energy Development
abstract: As electric vehicle charging station operations become more common, proper coordination of energy management is necessary to avoid high operational costs and carbon emissions caused by electric vehicle charging requirements, intermittent renewable sources, and fluctuating electricity rates. In this research, a forecast-based optimization methodology is created with the objective of optimizing the charge-discharge management of a renewable-powered electric vehicle charging station system involving photovoltaic generation, wind generation, fuel cells, electric vehicles, and stationary batteries. First, a recurrent neural network is used to predict relevant time series data, such as photovoltaic energy, wind energy, electric vehicle load demand, fuel cell energy production, and electric vehicle energy consumption. These forecasted data are then applied to a bi-objective energy management optimization problem, which is solved using NSGA-II. The objective is to minimize operating cost and emissions while considering power balance, grid energy exchange, and other operational constraints associated with the fuel cell, battery storage system, and electric vehicles. In this study, two scenarios are examined using one month of hourly data; Scenario 1 does not use stationary batteries, whereas Scenario 2 uses them. The forecasting results show robust predictions, with one-hour-ahead values ranging from 0.9162 to 0.9708. The optimization results show that Scenario 2 provides better energy shifting and peak-period support through battery charging and discharging management. Compared with Scenario 1, the operating cost is reduced from $171,833.86 to $160,388.44, and emissions are decreased from 13,485.48 kg to 12,892.23 kg, leading to 6.7% and 4.4% reductions, respectively.

title: Workforce Aging and Firm Productivity: Evidence from Türkiye
journal: Review of Middle East Economics and Finance
abstract: Abstract Does workforce aging lower firm productivity? We study this question for a large emerging economy using matched employer–employee records from Türkiye linked to firm balance sheets over 2013–2023, roughly 1.75 million firm–year observations. Identifying the relationship from within-firm variation, we find that a higher share of older workers is associated with modestly lower productivity: a one-unit increase in the share of workers aged 50 and above lowers value added per worker by about 8.3 %. Much of the larger raw correlation reflects sorting of younger workforces into more productive firms, but a precise negative effect survives selection. The average conceals pronounced heterogeneity: the penalty is about 11 % in manufacturing and routine-intensive services, roughly half as large in construction and trade, and statistically absent in agriculture. Interacting the firm’s age composition with task scores confirms the mechanism: the penalty is attenuated where non-routine interpersonal content is high and amplified where routine and analytical content are high. What matters is less the age of a workforce than the work it performs. This is among the first firm-level evidence on aging and productivity for a large emerging economy.

title: Whole-Body Effect Profiles of Acupoints: A Profile-Centric Framework for Specificity
When do consumers respond to ASMR-based retail advertising in Taiwan? The boundary role of ASMR responsiveness
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
abstract: Purpose This study examines how Taiwanese consumers respond to autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR)-based retail advertising. It proposes a bounded sensory-affective persuasion framework in which ASMR responsiveness functions as a consumer-level boundary condition, rather than assuming that ASMR cues are universally persuasive. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 626 Taiwanese consumers were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. A separate within-subject EEG pilot experiment involving 18 participants was used only as a supplementary physiological check on frontal α-band patterns during advertising exposure; repeated trials were treated as within-participant observations, not as an enlarged participant-level sample. Findings Affective mechanism and brand awareness positively predicted purchase intention, which in turn predicted anticipated purchase behavior. ASMR responsiveness negatively moderated the relationship between affective mechanism and purchase intention, indicating attenuation rather than reversal of the positive effect. The cognitive-load-based moderated moderation was not supported. The EEG pilot showed no statistically significant omnibus effects of cognitive load, ASMR exposure, or their interaction on frontal a activity. Accordingly, the EEG component is interpreted cautiously as supplementary descriptive context rather than as confirmatory evidence. Originality/value The study advances sensory marketing and Asia-Pacific retail advertising research by showing that consumer responses to ASMR-based retail advertising in Taiwan depend on individual ASMR responsiveness and on whether sensory-affective experiences are converted into purchase-related evaluation.

title: Ultrasound-Assisted Alkaline Extraction of Soluble Dietary Fiber from Cucumber Pomace: Structural Modification, Hydration Properties and In Vitro Glucose and Cholesterol Adsorption Capacities
Towards the learning estate: from digital–physical to experience orchestration
abstract: Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

title: The enabling role of the INTOSAI development initiative to audit SDGs for public value in the Western Balkans
abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore the enabling role of the International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions’ (INTOSAI) Development Initiative (IDI) to audit sustainable development goals (SDGs) and embed public value thinking within a transitional Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) context of the Western Balkans (Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia). Design/methodology/approach The paper is built on a qualitative research design; empirical data were obtained by conducting ad hoc interviews with IDI experts on SDGs auditing and auditing experts in the Western Balkans, complemented with secondary data analysis. To analyse the empirical data, the authors applied Moore’s Strategic Triangle (1995, 2013), which offers a more nuanced perspective on what constitutes value-driven public accountability, legitimacy, trust and the operational capacity of a transitional SAIs context. Findings The transition from compliance-based to performance auditing, including the more recent and more complex practice of SDGs auditing, is becoming more broadly institutionalised across many transitional SAIs contexts, including the Western Balkans. The authors presented IDI’s enabling role in supporting SAIs in emerging economies in their SDGs auditing by enhancing their professional capacity, institutional legitimacy and accountability mechanisms. Still, the authors also empirically observe that the shift towards public value orientation, focused on legitimacy, trust, professional capacity, collective outcomes and societal well-being, remains at an early stage in the Western Balkans. It also reveals that public value creation involves balancing competing demands, reconciling global expectations with national priorities and reforms and navigating resource asymmetries and competing stakeholders’ expectations. Originality/value This paper contributes by offering a nuanced perspective on the conceptual and empirical development of SDGs auditing within transitional SAIs contexts. It highlights IDI’s enabling role in supporting SAIs in transitional contexts to embed public value thinking into their audit frameworks, while maintaining methodological rigour and adherence to internationally recognised sustainability assurance standards.

title: Team Teaching for Maternal and Child Health Preparation Among Assistant Medical Officer Trainees: Confidence and Competency Outcomes
abstract: Background: Assistant Medical Officer (AMO) trainees are expected to perform maternal and child health (MCH) procedures safely during clinical placement, yet confidence may remain low when earlier exposure is fragmented. Methods: This single-group quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study evaluated a structured team-teaching intervention among 52 Semester 5 (Year 3 Semester I) trainees at the Training Institute, Ministry of Health Malaysia (ILKKM) Kota Kinabalu. The intervention involved two days of supervised practice covering 11 MCH procedures aligned with the Clinical Practice IV module. Competency was assessed during the structured training using the national Diploma in Medical and Health Sciences (DMHS) rubric, while confidence and satisfaction were measured using a content-validated questionnaire. The pre-intervention confidence assessment was conducted before team teaching, while the post-intervention confidence assessment was administered after trainees completed their subsequent two-week MCH clinical placement. Paired-sample t-tests were used to compare pre- and post-confidence scores. Results: Mean self-perceived confidence scores increased from 2.31 ± 0.36 after the team-teaching intervention and subsequent MCH clinical posting (p < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen’s dz = 3.02). Most trainees demonstrated competency at Scores 3 and 4 across the assessed procedures. Positive responses to the three principal satisfaction indicators ranged from 90.4% to 94.2%. The findings indicate increased self-perceived confidence following the structured training and subsequent clinical exposures, alongside generally high competency performance and positive perceptions of the learning experience. Conclusion: Structured team teaching combined with subsequent clinical exposure was associated with increased self-perceived confidence, while trainees demonstrated generally high competency during procedural assessment. The approach may support competency-based preparation within AMO training programmes, although further comparative evaluation is required to determine the specific contribution of team teaching.

title: Social impacts of disasters in South Korea: A systematic literature review
abstract: Given the increasing frequency and complexity of disasters in South Korea, there is a growing need to strengthen forward-looking and effective disaster management. South Korea has concentrated on managing physical impacts, but disasters can have both physical and social impacts. This research aimed to examine creative and feasible alternatives for addressing the social impacts of disasters in the field of South Korean disaster management. Based on a systematic literature review (to include PRISMA 2020 guidelines) as a major methodology, three periods of social impacts of disasters (as analytical categories) were analyzed by cross-checking three analytical levels (as analytical units): Individual, community, and national, as well as four aspects of social impacts (as analytical units): Psychological hurt, unequal minority, unemployment disadvantages, and political battle. The key theme was that the social impacts of disasters evolved or may evolve into social ignorance (July 1953–May 2004), social complaint (June 2004–April 2014), and social awareness (from May 2014 onwards), in chronological order. This article comprehensively examines the social impacts of disasters on dynamic South Korea, surpassing previous studies.
